title: Task scheduler requirements
idea: Scoping a task scheduler means fixing what a task is, when it runs, which task wins a tie, what happens when it fails, and what v1 leaves out.
points: A task pairs a job with a run time and a priority.
Due tasks run earliest first; a tie goes to the higher priority.
A failed task retries after a growing delay, up to a set limit.
Assume one process, many thousands of tasks, and an injectable clock for tests.

hero.title: Actors and use cases in v1

edges.caption: A client hands over a job, a run time, a priority and an optional repeat period.
The client gets a task id back. It uses that id to cancel or read status.
Time is an actor: once a task's run time passes, it becomes due.

edges.label: queues
edges.caption: Submitted tasks wait in order of run time, then priority.

edges.label: on failure
edges.caption: A job that throws goes back into the queue with a later run time.
Surviving a restart, task dependencies and cron syntax wait for later. Name them out loud.

code.title: Scope and run order
code.caption: The v1 scope as an enum you can read aloud, and the ordering rule tested on three tasks.

walk.text: Print every use case with its actor and an IN or OUT tag.
Three tasks: two share a run time, one is earlier.
The ordering rule: run time ascending, then priority descending.
Six use cases form v1: two kinds of submit, cancel, query, run and retry.
Three are named and cut, so the boundary is part of the design.

pitfalls: Ask whether higher priority can jump ahead of an earlier run time; usually it cannot.
Agree on retry limits and backoff before writing code; unlimited retries hide bugs.
State that v1 lives in memory; persistence across restarts is a separate decision.

quiz.q: Two tasks are due at the same moment. Which rule should v1 state first?
options: Run whichever task was submitted last
Higher priority first, then earlier submission
Run both at once on separate threads, always
Pick one at random to keep things fair
quiz.why: A clear, deterministic tie-break makes the order testable. Priority first, then submit order, gives every pair of tasks one defined order.

takeaway: Fix run time, priority order and the retry rule before any class.

starters: Should priority ever override an earlier run time?
What is the difference between fixed rate and fixed delay?
Why inject a clock instead of calling System.currentTimeMillis?
